new_statements.quote: 11.—Un point très important de la phonétique nahanaise est l'hiatus que je rends par le point en haut (˙). Il a pour effet de faire hausser la voix sur la syllabe qui le précède et de couper, pour ainsi dire, le mot en deux [...]. 12.—Enfin le nahanais possède un accent très clairement défini marqué du signe ʹ qui fait appuyer considérablement sur la syllabe qui en est affectée. Cet accent très sensible dans certains mots, surtout ceux d'origine tlinket, est moins apparent chez d'autres sur la désinence desquels il se porte tout particulièrement.
new_statements.translation: 11.—A very important point of Nahanais phonetics is the hiatus [glottal catch], which I render by the raised dot (˙). Its effect is to raise the voice on the syllable preceding it and, so to speak, to cut the word in two [...]. 12.—Finally, Nahanais has a very clearly defined accent, marked with the sign ʹ, which makes one bear down considerably on the syllable affected by it. This accent, very perceptible in certain words, above all those of Tlingit origin, is less apparent in others, on whose ending [final syllable] it falls most particularly.
new_statements.citation: [Morice, Adrien-Gabriel]. [1899]. Précis de grammaire nahanaise: phonétique nahanaise. S.l.: s.n., 72 pp. (MPG PuRe item_403671; CIHM 18392).
new_statements.locator: Article premier (Phonétique nahanaise), 'Des sons', §12 (with §11), printed p. 5 = PDF p. 3 of the MPG scan
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again., PDF p.3 = printed p.5, 'Des Sons' §§11-12, read from the page image (the scanned layer is garbled but the scan is clear). §11 and §12 are there word for word as quoted; the reader's [..] elides only the end of §11 ('en interrompant brusquement la prononciation de la syllabe qui peut le suivre') and its small-print note ('Préfixé à un mot.. suffixé à une désinence, il fait élever le ton et occasionne un arrêt subit de la voix sur cette désinence'). Translation is fair. IDENTITY (fails): the Précis does not describe Kaska. I downloaded Morice's published account, 'The Nah·ane and their language', Trans. Canadian Institute 7 (1902-3 [1904]): 517-534 (archive.o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Morice, native words carry a (weakly realized) accent on the word ending, i.e. the final syllable (which in Athabaskan nouns/verbs is the stem); in some words, especially Tlingit loanwords, the accent is much more salient and Morice marks its position lexically with ʹ. Modern descriptions instead treat Kaska as a tone language (marked high tone; long vowels also rising/falling) and give no stress-placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Words of Tlingit origin have a strongly audible accent (position marked word by word); §11: a glottal 'hiatus' raises the pitch of the preceding syllable (a tone/glottalization effect, not stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, impressionistic 1899 missionary description of 'nahanais'; final-syllable reading could equally be read as stem (morphologically determined) prominence. Meek 2001:105 (Pelly Banks/Liard Kaska) presupposes stress ('[ɛ] and [ɪ] in unstressed positions'; 'vowel length may be phonemic, due to stress..') but never locates it and states 'Kaska is also a tonal language, having high, low, rising and falling tones'; Moore & Tuttle 2003 describe phonemic high tone, declination and phrase-final lengthening only.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes 'le nahanais' — Morice's Nah·ane, his cover term for the Tahltan–Kaska(–Tagish) 'Nahane' Dene; MPG PuRe (ISO kkz), CIHM and Glottolog all catalogue the work under Kaska, but the ms. itself names no consultants, locality or dialect. Internal cues point at least partly toward Tahltan (tahl1239) or a Stikine/Dease-area variety rather than Yukon Kaska: Morice says Nahanais has only one nasal vowel ('an'), whereas Kaska has a full nasal series, and gives 'lue' for 'fish' (Tahltan łuwe; Kaska łūge, cf. 'Łūge łēt'e' in the 1994 Ross River curriculum). A reviewer should resolve this (e.g. via Morice 1904) before filing the statement under kask1239. The modern Kaska sources read (Meek 2001: Pelly Banks with Liard/Stone data; Moore & Tuttle 2003; YNLC Yukon dialects) are unambiguously Kaska but give no stress-placement rule.

new_statements.quote: 12.—Enfin le nahanais possède un accent très clairement défini marqué du signe ' qui fait appuyer considérablement sur la syllabe qui en est affectée. Cet accent très sensible dans certains mots, surtout ceux d'origine tlinket, est moins apparent chez d'autres sur la désinence desquels il se porte tout particulièrement. [§11:] Un point très important de la phonétique nahanaise est l'hiatus que je rends par le point en haut (˙). Il a pour effet de faire hausser la voix sur la syllabe qui le précède et de couper, pour ainsi dire, le mot en deux, en interrompant brusquement la prononciation de la syllabe qui peut le suivre.
new_statements.translation: 12.—Finally, Nahane has a very clearly defined accent, marked by the sign ', which makes one bear down considerably on the syllable it affects. This accent, very perceptible in certain words, especially those of Tlingit origin, is less apparent in others, on whose final syllable (désinence) it falls most particularly. [§11:] A very important point of Nahane phonetics is the hiatus, which I render by the raised dot (˙). Its effect is to raise the voice on the syllable that precedes it and to cut the word, so to speak, in two, abruptly interrupting the pronunciation of the syllable that may follow it.
new_statements.citation: Morice, Adrien G. (1899). Précis de grammaire nahanaise. 77 pp.
new_statements.locator: Article premier, Phonétique nahanaise, 'Des sons', §11 and §12 with its small-type note, printed p. 5 = PDF p. 3 (verified on the page image)
new_statements.relation_note: This is the source of the existing statement itself; the full §12 note (not in the truncated existing quote) adds that the accent is most audible in Tlingit-origin words and otherwise falls particularly on the désinence. The existing reading label 'tone language, no stress statement' is not what the text says: Morice does make an accent statement (lexically marked, final-syllable tendency), never uses the word 'tone' for the accent (only 'fait élever le ton' for the hiatus). Identity caveat: the text never names the variety; Morice 1904 p. 518 places the collection of his grammatical material at Thalhthan (Tahltan). The [1899] date is a catalogue bracket and sits uneasily with Morice 1904's…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A clearly defined accent written with an apostrophe-like sign on the syllable it affects, i.e. lexically marked in the orthography rather than predicted by a rule; strongest in Tlingit loanwords; in other (native) words it is weaker and falls 'tout particulièrement' on the désinence (the word-final syllable/ending). The hiatus (glottal stop, raised dot) additionally raises the voice (pitch) on the preceding syllable, and, suffixed to an ending, 'fait élever le ton'. Read together with Morice 1904 (same accent, described there as lengthening + raised pitch), this is a lexically distributed pitch/length prominence, i.e. what later work treats as Tahltan/Kaska tone; Morice's own wording ('appuyer') is a stress/intensity description.
new_statements.exceptions: accent 'moins apparent' in words not of Tlingit origin; no other exceptions stated
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Morice's 'Western Nah'ane', i.e. the Thalhthan/Tahltan of the Stikine (Glottolog tahl1239), not Kaska proper. Morice 1904 p. 518: the material for 'a grammatical compendium' (the Précis) was gathered on his trip to Thalhthan; p. 527: the accent is a feature of 'the Western Nah'ane', attributed to contact with the Tlingit of Fort Wrangell; pp. 519-520: the Kaska are the 'third division' (Dease/Upper Liard/Frances Lake), whom the Thalhthan said 'spoke exactly the same language as themselves, with, of course, some local peculiarities'. The Précis names no variety. Glottolog/MPG file both under Kaska (kkz); the attribution to kask1239 therefore rests on cataloguing, and any catalog entry built on these two works should be labelled Tahltan (Western Nah'ane) or at most 'Tahltan-Kaska per Morice'. Modern Kaska sources held by the project from the earlier reading (Moore & Tuttle 2003 handout; Meek 2001 p. 105 'Kaska is also a tonal language'; YNLC alphabet with high/low/rising/falling tone marks) treat Kaska as tonal and say nothing about word stress.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the two sources: both describe the same lexically marked accent (Précis §12: written with ', 'fait appuyer considérablement', strongest in Tlingit loans, otherwise tending to the désinence; 1904 pp. 527-528: lengthens the syllable and raises pitch, present on some monosyllables and not others, initial in tène 'man'). The only tension is with the existing_statements label 'tone language, no stress statement': Morice never calls it tone; he describes an accent with pitch, length and intensity effects and no positional rule, which is best filed as a lexically distributed pitch accent (in modern terms almost certainly the Tahltan/Kaska high tone). The 'regular accent' phrase means 'consistently present', not 'fixed in position': monosyllables with and without it, first syllable in tène, final in kussa'. The larger issue is identity, not placement (see the note on which variety).
